text: Everything so far in this chapter assumed a clean, mostly cloud-native environment — labeled workloads, a ZTNA broker, cloud subscription roles. Most real enterprises aren't that clean. Almost every organization that adopted cloud over the last decade still runs an on-premises Active Directory domain somewhere, and this lesson is about what happens when those two worlds have to be governed as one.

Treating on-prem AD and cloud identity as two separately-managed security programs creates a real gap, not just an administrative headache. A domain admin credential that's tightly controlled in the cloud tenant but loosely controlled on-premises is still a domain admin credential, and an attacker compromising it doesn't care which side of that boundary they came in from. Unifying the two starts with unifying the identity itself.

Microsoft Entra Connect is the real mechanism most enterprises use for that: it syncs on-prem AD accounts, group memberships, and password hashes into Microsoft Entra ID, so a user has exactly one identity both sides recognize. Built on that sync, hybrid Conditional Access and Entra's Application Proxy let the same identity-and-device policy govern an on-prem application that it governs a cloud one — one policy engine, one identity, regardless of which side of the boundary the resource sits on.

Identity sync alone doesn't fix on-prem privilege, though. Microsoft's documented AD tiering model splits privileged access into Tier 0 — domain controllers and identity infrastructure — Tier 1 servers, and Tier 2 workstations, with a hard rule that a credential valid at one tier can never log onto a system at a more sensitive tier. It's the same blast-radius logic as Lesson 9's micro-segmentation, now applied to on-prem privilege levels instead of network traffic.

That rule only holds if a Tier 0 credential is never typed on a less-trusted machine, because malware on that machine can capture it the instant it's entered. A Privileged Access Workstation — hardened, single-purpose, nothing else running on it — is how the tiering rule gets enforced at the device level instead of staying a policy on paper. Identity sync, hybrid Conditional Access, tiering, and PAWs together are what turn two separate security programs into one. That closes out least privilege and micro-segmentation — Chapter 4 picks up from here with assume-breach design.
